principle: A Pin Gains Value From the Target Behind It
rule: Evaluate a pin by what becomes vulnerable if the pinned piece moves, not by the mere fact that it cannot move freely.

principle: Use Skewers Against High-Value Front Pieces
rule: Attack a valuable front piece so its forced movement exposes a less valuable but capturable unit behind it.

principle: Discovered Attacks Release Hidden Force
rule: Move the blocking piece with tempo so a rook, bishop, or queen attacks through the newly opened line.

principle: Double Attacks Win Through Reply Shortage
rule: Create two independent threats that cannot both be met by one move.

principle: Clearance Creates Access
rule: Vacate a square, file, rank, or diagonal so another piece can use it immediately.

principle: Interference Breaks Defensive Communication
rule: Place a piece between a defender and its target to sever the line of protection.

principle: X-Ray Pressure Persists Through an Occupied Line
rule: Notice attacks that would exist if an intervening piece moved or were exchanged.

principle: Attract a Piece Onto a Tactical Line
rule: Use a forcing offer or check to draw a king or piece onto a square where another tactic becomes possible.

principle: Use the Desperado Before Losing a Trapped Piece
rule: When a piece is certain to be lost, seek checks, captures, or structural damage before allowing its removal.

principle: Consider Underpromotion When Queen Promotion Fails
rule: Check whether promotion to a rook, bishop, or knight avoids stalemate or creates a unique tactical effect.

principle: Visualize the Position After Every Forcing Move
rule: Rebuild the board mentally after each move instead of carrying an outdated image forward.

principle: Branch Where the Opponent Has Real Choices
rule: Create calculation branches only at replies that materially change the outcome.

principle: Prune Dominated Candidates
rule: Stop analyzing a candidate when another move produces the same benefits with fewer concrete risks.

principle: Use Elimination When No Move Looks Best
rule: Reject candidates with concrete defects until the most resilient option remains.

principle: Calculate Capture Order Precisely
rule: When several exchanges are possible, test different capture and recapture sequences.

principle: Maintain a Material Ledger
rule: Track material changes explicitly during long combinations.

principle: Recognize Transpositions in the Tree
rule: Notice when different move orders reach the same position and evaluate it once.

principle: Calculate Backward From the Desired Result
rule: When seeking mate, promotion, or a tactical construction, identify the required final geometry and work backward to enabling moves.

principle: Distinguish Forced Moves From Merely Natural Moves
rule: Label replies as forced only when all alternatives fail concretely.

principle: Use a Verification Pass Before Committing
rule: After selecting a move, inspect the line once from the opponent's perspective.

principle: Material Is Only One Evaluation Factor
rule: Balance material against king safety, activity, structure, space, and forcing initiative.

principle: King Safety Is a Dynamic Quantity
rule: Judge king safety by accessible lines, attacking force, defenders, and escape squares rather than pawn appearance alone.

principle: Activity Can Outweigh Structural Damage
rule: Accept a structural defect when it produces sustained piece activity or open lines that the opponent cannot neutralize.

principle: Space Needs a Conversion Method
rule: Value extra territory by the piece improvements and pawn breaks it enables.

principle: The Initiative Belongs to the Side Asking Questions
rule: Identify which side creates threats that force replies and how long that sequence can continue.

principle: Separate Static and Dynamic Advantages
rule: Classify advantages by whether they persist automatically or require immediate energetic play.

principle: Choose Which Imbalance to Play Around
rule: Select the material, structural, spatial, or piece-quality difference most capable of producing a plan.

principle: Evaluate Both Sides' Worst Pieces
rule: Compare the least effective piece on each side and the ease with which it can improve.

principle: A Weakness Requires Access
rule: Call a pawn or square weak only when the opponent can reach and exploit it without excessive cost.

principle: Compare Plans by Their Counterplay
rule: Evaluate a plan partly by the opponent's strongest active response.

principle: Trade One Advantage for a More Usable One
rule: Convert temporary activity, space, or initiative into material, structure, or a favorable ending before it fades.

principle: Simplify Into the Right Endgame
rule: Exchange pieces only after identifying the concrete winning or drawing mechanism in the resulting ending.

principle: Change the Pawn Structure to Favor Your Pieces
rule: Use exchanges or breaks that open lines for your good pieces and restrict the opponent's.

principle: Convert an Attack Into a Positional Gain
rule: When mate is unavailable, use the attack to win a pawn, damage structure, gain the bishop pair, or dominate key squares.

principle: Switch Wings When the Defender Overconcentrates
rule: Transfer pressure to the opposite side after enemy pieces become tied to one wing.

principle: Restrain Before You Blockade
rule: Stop enemy pawn mobility before occupying the ideal blockading square.

principle: Blockade Before You Attack the Base
rule: Immobilize an advanced pawn or chain before redirecting force toward its support.

principle: Accumulate Advantages That Support Each Other
rule: Prefer small gains that combine into one coherent plan.

principle: Remove Counterplay Before Converting
rule: Restrict checks, pawn breaks, and active piece routes before cashing in a material or positional advantage.

principle: Choose Multipurpose Improving Moves
rule: When no tactic is forced, favor moves that advance several useful goals simultaneously.

principle: Use the Minority Attack in the Carlsbad Structure
rule: Advance the queenside pawn minority to create a fixed weakness in the opponent's majority.

principle: Use the Isolated Pawn's Break Before Exchanges
rule: In isolated-queen-pawn positions, prepare the central advance while enough pieces remain to support activity.

principle: Hanging Pawns Need Mobility
rule: Keep connected c- and d-pawns capable of advancing together or supporting a central break.

principle: The Maroczy Bind Restrains Pawn Breaks
rule: Use pawns on c4 and e4 to limit the opponent's freeing ...d5 break while improving pieces behind the space.

principle: French Chains Create Opposite-Wing Plans
rule: Follow the locked central chain toward the wing where your space points and attack the chain's base from the other side.

principle: King's Indian Centers Create a Race
rule: In a closed King's Indian structure, compare White's queenside break with Black's kingside break by tempo.

principle: Hedgehog Positions Depend on Timed Breaks
rule: In a restrained setup, prepare ...b5 or ...d5 until tactical conditions make the release favorable.

principle: Stonewall Structures Trade Squares for Stability
rule: Use the dark-square grip and e4 outpost while accounting for weakened light squares and the restricted bishop.

principle: Opposite-Wing Majorities Create Two Fronts
rule: Use your pawn majority to create a passer while restraining the opponent's majority on the other wing.

principle: Create Piece Imbalances in Symmetrical Structures
rule: When pawns are symmetrical, seek differences in activity, open-file control, minor-piece quality, or king placement.

principle: Challenge the Base of a Fianchetto
rule: Attack the pawn and bishop complex supporting a fianchettoed king rather than sacrificing automatically on the shelter.

principle: Exchange Sacrifices Need Positional Returns
rule: Give a rook for a minor piece only when the resulting squares, pawns, king exposure, or domination provide durable compensation.

principle: Use an Open Rook-Pawn File Against the King
rule: Place a rook or queen on an opened h- or a-file when it leads directly to the castled king.

principle: Control Flight Squares Before Checking
rule: Build a mating net by restricting the king's destinations before spending checks.

principle: Bring the Worst Attacker Into the Attack
rule: Before forcing matters, improve the attacking piece contributing least.

principle: Offer a Queen Trade to Break the Attack
rule: When defending, use a queen exchange threat to force the attacker to lose time or abandon key squares.

principle: Blockade the Pawn Storm
rule: Stop attacking pawns on fixed squares before they can open files against your king.

principle: Counter-Sacrifice to Remove the Initiative
rule: Return or invest material to open escape squares, trade attackers, or seize forcing counterplay.

principle: Perpetual Check Is an Active Defensive Resource
rule: Search for repeated checking geometry when material defense is impossible.

principle: Defend the Entry Square, Not Every Attacked Pawn
rule: Prioritize the invasion point that would make the opponent's pressure decisive.

principle: Knights Struggle Against Distant Passed Pawns
rule: Create or support passers far from an enemy knight's current zone.

principle: Bishops Gain Value on Both Wings
rule: Keep play on both flanks when your bishop can switch faster than the opponent's knight or king.

principle: Opposite-Colored Bishops Favor the Defender
rule: Expect drawing chances when each bishop controls squares the other cannot challenge, especially with pawns on one wing.

principle: Opposite-Colored Bishops Strengthen Middlegame Attacks
rule: With queens or rooks present, attack on the color controlled by your bishop and inaccessible to the opponent's bishop.

principle: Fix Pawns on the Color Your Bishop Can Attack
rule: Place or induce enemy pawns onto squares accessible to your bishop before entering the ending.

principle: Put Your Pawns Opposite Your Own Bishop's Color
rule: When practical, place pawns on squares your bishop does not occupy so they do not block it.

principle: A Knight Needs an Active King
rule: Use the king to protect the knight's outpost and address distant threats.

principle: Use Triangulation to Lose a Tempo
rule: Maneuver the king or bishop in a loop to return to the same position with the opponent to move.

principle: Create Zugzwang by Removing Useful Moves
rule: Restrict pawn and piece moves until every legal reply concedes a square or pawn.

principle: Sacrifice a Minor Piece for the Last Pawns When It Draws
rule: Give the piece for all remaining enemy pawns if the opponent cannot mate with the material left.

principle: Cut Off the Enemy King With the Rook
rule: Use a rook along a rank or file to deny the king access before pursuing pawns.

principle: Build the Lucena Bridge
rule: In the standard rook-and-pawn win, use rook checks and shielding to escort the king from the promotion file.

principle: Use the Philidor Third-Rank Defense
rule: Keep the defending rook active on the third rank until the stronger king advances, then check from behind.

principle: Check From the Side With Adequate Distance
rule: Use lateral rook checks when at least several files separate the rook from the king.

principle: Know the Wrong-Bishop Rook-Pawn Draw
rule: Recognize that a bishop unable to control the pawn's promotion corner may not win with a rook pawn.

principle: Centralize the Queen With Tempo
rule: Use checks and attacks to bring the queen toward the center without allowing counterchecks.

principle: King Safety Dominates Queen Endgames
rule: Evaluate checking networks and perpetuals before counting pawns.

principle: Build a Perpetual-Check Map
rule: Identify a repeatable set of checking squares before beginning the sequence.

principle: Calculate Queen Trades to the Final Pawn Ending
rule: Before offering or accepting a queen trade, calculate the resulting king-and-pawn position exactly.

principle: Connected Passed Pawns Can Outweigh a Rook
rule: Coordinate connected advanced passers so the rook cannot stop both without help.

principle: Treat the Clock as a Strategic Resource
rule: Budget time according to decision importance and preserve enough for later tactical phases.

principle: Use the Opponent's Time to Think
rule: During the opponent's turn, update threats, evaluate likely candidates, and plan your response.

principle: Reset Emotion After a Blunder
rule: Accept the new position and solve its problems instead of trying to undo the previous move emotionally.

principle: Play the Position, Not the Rating
rule: Choose moves from board evidence rather than fear of a stronger opponent or contempt for a weaker one.

principle: Choose Practical Complexity When the Match Requires It
rule: When a draw is insufficient, prefer sound positions with more decisions and winning chances.

principle: Reduce Variance When a Draw Is Valuable
rule: When tournament circumstances favor a draw, choose sound simplifications that preserve equality and remove unnecessary tactical risk.

principle: Respond to Opening Surprises With Fundamentals
rule: When theory ends unexpectedly, restore center, development, king safety, and threat awareness before improvising.

principle: Evaluate Draw Offers From the Position
rule: Consider objective evaluation, clock, match needs, and practical risk before accepting or declining.

principle: Create Difficult Choices for the Opponent
rule: Among sound moves, prefer those that preserve your plan while forcing the opponent to solve non-obvious problems.

principle: Use a Between-Round Reset Routine
rule: Recover physically and mentally before beginning deep analysis or the next game.

principle: Train Visualization Without Moving Pieces
rule: Practice maintaining piece locations and lines through short sequences in your head.

principle: Keep a Calculation Notebook
rule: Write candidate trees, evaluations, and errors so calculation quality becomes measurable.

principle: Study Model Games by Structure
rule: Group instructive games by pawn skeleton and recurring plan rather than only by player or opening name.

principle: Interleave Different Skill Types
rule: Mix tactics, strategy, endgames, and calculation once basic patterns are learned.

principle: Retrieve Before You Review
rule: Attempt to recall the move, plan, or explanation before reopening notes.

principle: Measure Error Frequency, Not Just Puzzle Rating
rule: Track recurring failure types and how often they appear in games.

principle: Train Difficult Defensive Positions
rule: Practice finding resources in worse positions instead of studying only winning combinations.

principle: Use Endgames to Sharpen Calculation
rule: Study reduced-material positions where move order, opposition, and races can be verified exactly.

principle: Teach the Principle in Your Own Words
rule: Explain an idea, its mechanism, and an exception without copying the source language.

principle: Build a Personal Decision Checklist
rule: Create a short sequence of questions based on your most frequent errors and use it consistently.
